specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain how the structure of the nervous system is adapted to its functions.
The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.

Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system (CNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

Students should be able to explain how the various structures in a reflex arc – including the sensory neurone, synapse, relay neurone and motor neurone – relate to their function. Students should understand why reflex actions are important.
Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; they do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
Students should be able to extract and interpret data from graphs, charts and tables, about the functioning of the nervous system.
Students should be able to translate information about reaction times between numerical and graphical forms.

concepts.definition: The system of receptors, neurones and the central nervous system that enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.
A cell or structure that detects a stimulus, for example the light receptors in the retina or the temperature receptors in the skin.
A nerve cell that carries information as electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, and from the central nervous system to effectors.
The brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors to the information it receives from receptors.
A structure that brings about the response. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
The sequence stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, which describes how the body detects and responds to a change.
An automatic and rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
The pathway taken by an impulse in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the CNS → motor neurone → effector.
The junction between two neurones. A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

misconceptions.question: In a response to a stimulus, which structure brings about the response?
misconceptions.correct: The effector brings about the response: a muscle contracting or a gland secreting a hormone. The receptor only detects the stimulus.
misconceptions.misconception: The structure that detects the stimulus is also the structure that brings about the response.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Detection and response often happen in the same part of the body, such as the hand touching something hot, so students merge the two roles into one structure.
misconceptions.correction: Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so receptor and effector are different structures in the pathway stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.

misconceptions.question: Which parts of the nervous system make up the central nervous system?
misconceptions.correct: The brain and the spinal cord only.
misconceptions.misconception: The central nervous system includes all the nerves in the body, including those in the arms and legs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'nervous system' and 'central nervous system' are used loosely in everyday speech, and diagrams often show the brain, spinal cord and nerves in one colour.
misconceptions.correction: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. Neurones carrying impulses from receptors to the CNS, and from the CNS to effectors, are not part of the CNS.

misconceptions.question: How does information pass from one neurone to the next at a synapse?
misconceptions.correct: A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
misconceptions.misconception: The electrical impulse passes straight across the synapse from one neurone into the next.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that impulses are electrical and picture the reflex arc as one continuous wire, so the gap at the synapse is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Impulses travel along neurones as electrical impulses, but at a synapse a chemical diffuses across the gap and starts a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

misconceptions.question: Does a reflex action involve the conscious part of the brain?
misconceptions.correct: No. Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
misconceptions.misconception: A reflex happens because the person decides very quickly to move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The person is usually awake and aware of what happened, and they notice the movement, so they assume they chose it.
misconceptions.correction: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; they do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Awareness of what happened comes after the response, not before it.

misconceptions.question: Does the impulse in a reflex arc pass through the central nervous system?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The impulse passes through a relay neurone in the CNS, even though the conscious part of the brain is not involved.
misconceptions.misconception: Because a reflex is not conscious, the impulse does not pass through the central nervous system at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate the CNS with conscious thought, so 'not conscious' is read as 'not in the brain or spinal cord'.
misconceptions.correction: In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone. The CNS still coordinates the response; only the conscious part of the brain is not involved.

misconceptions.question: A student's mean reaction time falls from 0.30 s to 0.22 s after practice. What does this show?
misconceptions.correct: The student is reacting faster after practice, because a shorter time means a quicker response.
misconceptions.misconception: A larger reaction time value means a faster reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In most measurements a bigger number means 'more' or 'better', so a taller bar on a chart is read as a better performance.
misconceptions.correction: Reaction time is the time taken to respond, so the smaller the value the faster the response. On a bar chart or graph of reaction times, a lower bar or point shows the quicker reaction.

misconceptions.question: Can a gland be an effector?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
misconceptions.misconception: Only muscles can act as effectors.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The examples used most often, such as pulling a hand away or shivering, all involve movement, so glands are forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so a gland secreting a hormone is just as much an effector as a contracting muscle.

misconceptions.question: One student's reaction time improves over three trials. What can be concluded from this?
misconceptions.correct: That this student's reaction time improved over these three trials.
misconceptions.misconception: A pattern in one person's results shows what would happen for other people too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are used to drawing a single conclusion from a practical, and a clear trend in a small table looks convincing on its own.
misconceptions.correction: Data extracted from a graph, chart or table describe the individuals actually measured. A conclusion about the functioning of the nervous system in other people needs data from those people as well.

mcqs.stem: A single neurone carries impulses from a receptor in the toe to the spinal cord. Which statement best explains how this structure is adapted to its function?

options.text: It is long, so impulses reach the CNS quickly.
options.rationale: Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system, so one long cell carries the impulse the whole way to the spinal cord without delay.

options.text: It detects the stimulus and causes the response.
options.rationale: A student who believes the structure that detects a stimulus also produces the response treats the neurone as receptor and effector combined. In the pathway stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, the neurone only carries information; receptors detect and effectors respond.

options.text: It is part of the central nervous system.
options.rationale: A student who thinks all nerves belong to the CNS counts this neurone as part of it. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, so a neurone running from the toe to the spinal cord is not part of the CNS.

options.text: It carries the impulse without using the CNS.
options.rationale: A student who believes rapid responses bypass the CNS assumes the neurone works alone. Information from receptors passes to the CNS, which coordinates the response of effectors.

mcqs.stem: Effectors in the human body may be:

options.text: muscles contracting or glands secreting
options.rationale: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

options.text: receptors detecting light and sound levels
options.rationale: A student who merges the roles of receptor and effector picks the structure that detects the stimulus. Receptors detect stimuli; effectors bring about the response.

options.text: skeletal muscles moving bones at a joint
options.rationale: A student who believes only muscles can be effectors chooses an answer that leaves glands out. The specification states that effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

options.text: sense organs that detect and respond
options.rationale: A student who merges the roles of detecting and responding treats the sense organs that detect a stimulus as the structures that also bring about the response. Sense organs contain receptors that detect stimuli, while effectors — muscles or glands — bring about the response.

mcqs.stem: In a reflex arc, what is the function of the relay neurone?

options.text: It carries the impulse to the conscious brain.
options.rationale: A student who believes a reflex involves a quick decision looks for a route to the conscious brain. Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain.

options.text: It links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone in the CNS.
options.rationale: In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone that carries the impulse to the effector.

options.text: It carries the electrical impulse across the synapse.
options.rationale: A student who pictures the reflex arc as one continuous electrical wire thinks a neurone bridges the synapse. At a synapse a chemical diffuses across the gap and sets off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

options.text: It carries the impulse to the effector without the CNS.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a reflex misses out the CNS altogether places the whole pathway in the limb. The relay neurone is in the CNS; it is the conscious part of the brain, not the CNS, that is not involved.

mcqs.stem: Why is a reflex action important when a person touches a very hot object?

options.text: It gives the person time to decide how to act.
options.rationale: A student who believes reflexes involve a fast decision sees thinking time as the benefit. Reflex actions do not involve the conscious part of the brain, and any decision would slow the response down.

options.text: It keeps the impulse out of the nervous system.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a reflex bypasses the CNS treats that as the reason it is fast. The impulse still passes through a relay neurone in the CNS; speed comes from not involving the conscious part of the brain.

options.text: It is rapid and automatic, reducing injury.
options.rationale: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; the hand is moved away from the stimulus before the conscious part of the brain is involved, which limits the damage done.

options.text: It lets the receptor produce the response itself.
options.rationale: A student who merges receptor and effector assumes the skin acts on its own. Receptors detect the stimulus and effectors, such as the muscles of the arm, bring about the response.

mcqs.stem: A table shows one student's mean reaction time in three trials: trial 1, 0.28 s; trial 2, 0.24 s; trial 3, 0.21 s. What do these data show?

options.text: The reaction time fell across the trials.
options.rationale: Reading the values in order from the table shows a decrease from 0.28 s to 0.21 s, which is the pattern the data support.

options.text: The reaction time rose across all the trials.
options.rationale: A student who reads reaction time as a score rather than a time sees improvement as an increase. The values 0.28 s, 0.24 s and 0.21 s get smaller, so the reaction time fell.

options.text: The student reacted more slowly each time.
options.rationale: A student who believes a bigger number means a faster reaction reads a falling time as getting slower. Reaction time is the time taken to respond, so a smaller value means a quicker response.

options.text: The results apply to other students too.
options.rationale: A student who generalises from one person extends the trend to everyone. These data come from one student in three trials and describe only that student.

mcqs.stem: Four students have mean reaction times of 0.15 s, 0.22 s, 0.28 s and 0.31 s. These values are drawn as a bar chart. Which statement about the chart is correct?

options.text: The tallest bar is the fastest time.
options.rationale: A student who reads a taller bar as a better performance picks this. The tallest bar shows the longest reaction time, which is the slowest response.

options.text: The shortest bar is the slowest time.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a larger value means a faster reaction reads the shortest bar as the worst result. The shortest bar, 0.15 s, is the shortest time and so the fastest reaction.

options.text: The tallest bar shows the 0.31 s time.
options.rationale: Translating the numbers into graphical form, bar height is proportional to reaction time, so the largest value, 0.31 s, gives the tallest bar.

options.text: Each bar stands for the group as a whole.
options.rationale: A student who does not separate individual results from group results treats one bar as representing everyone. Each bar shows the mean reaction time of one named student.
